descs.t: Mary Peltola denies she knew of an effort to put a second Dan Sullivan on the Alaska Senate ballot beside Senator Dan Sullivan. The New York Times reports her campaign staff and Senate Democrats' campaign arm were involved, and the Justice Department has reportedly issued more than 30 grand jury subpoenas. We walk through what is reported, what is denied and what happens to the vote.

The Alaska Senate race now has a criminal investigation attached to it. Mary Peltola says she knew nothing about the decoy Dan Sullivan, while the New York Times reports her staff helped recruit him and House Oversight Chair James Comer says he is investigating. We look at the denial against the reporting, and at the governor's warning that the state may not certify the result.

Mary Peltola once said misleading voters should be a criminal offense. Now a second Dan Sullivan sits on Alaska's ballot, the New York Times ties her campaign to him, and federal subpoenas are reportedly flying. We lay out the evidence, her denial, and why a trick built to confuse voters is an attack on every voter's right to choose.

intro.plain: Mary Peltola says she knew nothing about the second Dan Sullivan on Alaska's Senate ballot. The New York Times reports her staff helped recruit him, and the Justice Department has reportedly issued more than 30 subpoenas. Days before the vote, that is a serious cloud over a race that could decide the Senate. So tell me in the chat: do you believe her denial?
intro.mid: Alaska's Senate race just turned into a criminal investigation. A second Dan Sullivan is on the ballot, the New York Times says Peltola's campaign helped put him there, and she says she knew nothing. The governor even says the state may not certify the result if she wins. Chat, if a decoy candidate changes the outcome, should the result stand?
intro.bold: Mary Peltola stood at a rally and said misleading voters should be a criminal offense. Now there is a fake Dan Sullivan on Alaska's ballot, the New York Times ties her campaign to him, and a grand jury is reportedly issuing subpoenas. She says she knew nothing. Chat, one word: is this a scandal or just hardball politics?

hook.plain: There are two Dan Sullivans on Alaska's Senate ballot, and only one is the senator. Here is what the reporting says, what Peltola denies, and what the subpoenas mean.
hook.mid: Peltola says she knew nothing. The New York Times says her staff found the second Dan Sullivan. Here is how the two stories collide, and what it does to the vote.
hook.bold: A candidate who called misleading voters a crime now faces reports her campaign planted a fake Dan Sullivan. Here is the evidence, and why it should worry every voter.

descs.t: The final Texas Senate poll from Quantus has Ken Paxton at 49.4 percent and James Talarico at 48.4 percent as early voting ends. The same poll has Greg Abbott ahead of Gina Hinojosa 52 to 46 for governor. We go through the numbers and what they say about turnout in Texas.

Ken Paxton leads James Talarico by one point in the final Texas Senate poll, while Greg Abbott leads by six for governor. Elon Musk has urged his followers to vote Paxton, and Talarico is running on healthcare for all. We look at why the Senate race is so much closer than the governor's race and what it means for control of the Senate.

Texas is one point from a Senate upset. The final Quantus poll has Ken Paxton at 49.4 percent and James Talarico at 48.4, with early voting closing and both sides pushing every last voter. We break down the race, the gap with the governor's contest, and what a Talarico win would mean.

intro.plain: The final Texas Senate poll is in: Ken Paxton 49.4 percent, James Talarico 48.4. That is one point, with early voting closing. For governor, Abbott leads Hinojosa by six. So the Senate race is the one to watch. Chat, are you in Texas, and did you vote early?
intro.mid: Texas, of all places, has a one point Senate race. Paxton 49.4, Talarico 48.4 in the final Quantus poll, while Abbott leads the governor's race by six. Elon Musk is telling his followers to vote Paxton. So why is Paxton running so far behind Abbott? Chat, give me your theory.
intro.bold: One point. That is all that separates Ken Paxton and James Talarico in the final Texas Senate poll, and early voting is closing. A Democrat winning a Texas Senate seat would shake up the whole map. Chat, call it now: does Paxton hold Texas or does Talarico pull the upset?

hook.plain: Paxton 49.4, Talarico 48.4. The final Texas Senate poll is a one point race. Here is what the numbers say and where the votes could still move.
hook.mid: Abbott leads Texas by six. Paxton leads by one. That gap tells you a lot about this Senate race, and here is what it means.
hook.bold: Texas is one point from a Senate upset. Here is how the race got this close, and what happens if it flips.

descs.t: An 80 hour ceasefire has allowed civilians to begin leaving Oleshky, a devastated town under Russian occupation. Russian and Ukrainian human rights ombudsmen are on the ground together, in a mission coordinated by First Lady Melania Trump. We go through how the evacuation is working and what has been delivered.

Civilians are leaving Russian occupied Oleshky under a ceasefire both sides credit to Melania Trump, and Putin has praised her role. But Kyiv's Center for Strategic Communications says Russian forces have begun taking civilians to Russia against the agreed terms. We look at what the mission achieved and what Kyiv says went wrong.

Oleshky was left in ruins under Russian occupation. Now an 80 hour truce is letting its people out, and Kyiv warns some are being taken to Russia instead of to safety. We walk through the evacuation, the Kremlin's media push around it, and why where these civilians end up matters.

intro.plain: Civilians are finally leaving Oleshky, a devastated town under Russian occupation. An 80 hour ceasefire, coordinated by Melania Trump, has Russian and Ukrainian human rights officials on the ground together, delivering aid and organising convoys. It is rare to see the two sides working side by side. Chat, do you think this kind of deal can lead anywhere bigger?
intro.mid: An 80 hour truce has opened a way out of Oleshky, and both Moscow and Kyiv are crediting Melania Trump. Putin even praised her. But Kyiv says Russian forces have started taking civilians into Russia, breaking the agreed terms. So is this a humanitarian win or a cover? Chat, what do you make of it?
intro.bold: Russia turned Oleshky into ruins. Now its officials are on camera taking part in the rescue, and Kyiv says some of those civilians are being taken to Russia rather than to safety. Melania Trump coordinated the ceasefire and Putin is praising her. Chat, is the Kremlin using a rescue as a propaganda stage?

hook.plain: For 80 hours the guns have gone quiet around Oleshky, and its people are getting out. Here is how the evacuation is working and who is running it.
hook.mid: Both Moscow and Kyiv credit Melania Trump for the Oleshky truce. But Kyiv says Russia is breaking the deal. Here is what is happening on the ground.
hook.bold: Russia ruined Oleshky. Now Kyiv says Russian forces are taking its civilians to Russia under cover of a ceasefire. Here is what the evacuation really looks like.

descs.t: Senator Chris Murphy says he was briefed on classified military planning against the Islamic Republic and calls the plan insane, without giving details. Reports say the Trump administration plans to strike after next week's midterm elections, with CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper briefing the President. We go through what Murphy said and what the reports claim.

Chris Murphy has gone public on a war plan he says he cannot describe, calling it insane and catastrophic days before the midterms. Reports say the administration plans to restart the war with the Islamic Republic after the vote. We look at what is confirmed, what is claimed, and why a senator would talk now.

A Democratic senator says the plan to restart the war on the Islamic Republic is insane. Reports say strikes could follow next week's midterms. We look at what Chris Murphy actually said, what the reports claim, and why real pressure on the regime is what its rulers fear most.

intro.plain: Senator Chris Murphy says he was briefed on classified plans for military action against the Islamic Republic, and he calls them insane, though he says he cannot share details. Reports say strikes could come after next week's midterms. So a lot is claimed and little is confirmed. Chat, do you think senators should go public on briefings like this?
intro.mid: Chris Murphy just did something unusual. He says he saw a classified war plan for the Islamic Republic, he cannot tell us what is in it, but he wants us to know it is insane. Reports say strikes could follow next week's midterms. Is this oversight, or is it campaigning? Chat, tell me which.
intro.bold: Chris Murphy says the plan to restart the war on the Islamic Republic is insane. Reports say strikes could come right after the midterms. If that is true, the people who should be most worried are the men running the regime. Chat, should Trump finish the job, yes or no?

hook.plain: A senator says he saw a classified war plan for the Islamic Republic and calls it insane. Here is what he said, and what the reports behind it claim.
hook.mid: Chris Murphy cannot tell you what is in the war plan, but he wants you to know it is insane. Here is why he is talking now, days before the vote.
hook.bold: A senator calls the next round against the Islamic Republic insane. The regime is listening. Here is what is reported, and why pressure works.

descs.t: The IRGC Navy says three tankers have caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, and says it is punishing ships that use unauthorized routes. UKMTO and security sources report limpet mines attached to a tanker overnight. We go through what is reported, what the IRGC claims, and what CENTCOM says about shipping.

Three tankers on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, by the IRGC's own account, while CENTCOM commander Admiral Brad Cooper says ships are flowing and the regime's oil exports are at zero. The Financial Times calls the limpet mine attacks an apparent tactical shift. We look at both claims and what it means for oil and for the war.

The IRGC is boasting about burning tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, after reports that its boats attached limpet mines to a ship in the protected lane. CENTCOM says the regime's navy is destroyed and its oil exports are at zero. We break down why sneak attacks on shipping are what a cornered regime does.

intro.plain: The IRGC Navy says three tankers have caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, and it says it is punishing ships that use unauthorized routes. Security sources report limpet mines attached to at least one tanker. At the same time CENTCOM says ships are flowing again. Chat, which side do you believe on Hormuz right now?
intro.mid: Two stories about the Strait of Hormuz today, and they do not match. CENTCOM's Admiral Cooper says ships are flowing and the regime's oil exports are at zero. The IRGC says three tankers are on fire. The FT calls the limpet mines a tactical shift. Chat, is Hormuz open or not?
intro.bold: The IRGC is putting out videos of tankers on fire in the Strait of Hormuz and calling it punishment. Reports say its boats slipped into the protected lane and stuck limpet mines on a ship. CENTCOM says the regime's navy is destroyed. Chat, is this a regime fighting back or one running out of moves?

hook.plain: Three tankers on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, by the IRGC's own count. Here is what is reported, how the attacks were carried out, and what it means for shipping.
hook.mid: CENTCOM says Hormuz is open. The IRGC says three tankers are burning. Here is how both can be true, and what it does to oil.
hook.bold: With its navy reportedly destroyed, the IRGC is sticking mines on tankers. Here is what that tells you about a regime under pressure.

descs.t: Opposition leader Rahul Gandhi says the Modi government sold IDBI Bank at a throwaway price. Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman says Congress has long used banks and financial institutions as personal entities, and government supporters call his claim a lie. We go through what each side says about the IDBI Bank sale.

The IDBI Bank sale has become a fight over history. Rahul Gandhi calls it a sale at a throwaway price, Nirmala Sitharaman answers with Congress's record of pressuring bank staff to lend, and Congress says it stands with IDBI employees. We look at the claims and the bigger question of who should own a bank.

Rahul Gandhi is attacking the sale of IDBI Bank, while the Finance Minister says Congress treated banks as personal entities and pushed staff to lend on a whim. We make the case that the scandal is a government owning a bank in the first place, and look at what each side claims about the sale.

intro.plain: There is a fight over the sale of IDBI Bank. Rahul Gandhi says the Modi government sold it at a throwaway price. Nirmala Sitharaman says Congress used banks as personal entities and pressured staff to hand out loans. Supporters of the government call his claim a lie. Chat, should governments be running banks at all?
intro.mid: Rahul Gandhi says IDBI Bank was sold off cheap. The Finance Minister answers with a history lesson on how Congress used banks, and Congress says it stands with IDBI employees. The real question underneath is who should own a bank. Chat, government or private, which do you trust with your money?
intro.bold: Rahul Gandhi is angry that IDBI Bank was sold. I think the real scandal is that a government ever ran it. The Finance Minister says Congress pressured bank staff to lend on a whim. That is exactly what happens when politicians own banks. Chat, agree or disagree?

hook.plain: Rahul Gandhi says IDBI Bank went for a throwaway price. The government says that is a lie. Here is what each side claims.
hook.mid: A bank sale has turned into a fight over decades of history. Here is the IDBI row, and the question nobody is asking.
hook.bold: When politicians own banks, loans follow politics. The IDBI fight shows why, and here is the case for getting government out.
